newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Vanclief sees low risk of grain delays.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Vanclief sees low risk of grain delays.

text.p: Canadian Agriculture Minister Lyle Vanclief said Monday there's a low risk of grain shipment delays in the 1997/98 (Aug/July) crop year similar to the one that bedeviled Canada from January to March of this year.

"They (grain and rail industry) are working on an early warning system, the rail cars that will be needed this year are already in the system, the railways are talking of different use of tracks," Vanclief told reporters here.
Transport Minister David Collenette and Canadian Wheat Board Minister Ralph Goodale and Vanclief met Friday with rail and grain officials. Vanclief remained in Winnipeg Monday.
They agreed to hold an early review of the transport system. It had been scheduled for 1999. The review now could begin as early mid-September.

In the meantime, an industry group was drafting a contingency plan and an early warning system designed to spark an early alert to the industry of problems such as those experienced early in 1997, he said.
More than 1.5 million tonnes of grain shipments were delayed from January to March causing a backlog of ships on Canada's west coast, with one vessel waiting as long as 62 days to load.
The Canadian Wheat Board faces more than C$15 million in demurrage fines as a result of the delays.
It lodged a complaint with the Canadian Transportation Agency against Canadian National Railway Co and CP Rail System.
The review of rail freight caps on grains cannot happen until the CTA rules on the CWB's complaint, Vanclief said.
The railways blamed heavy snowfall, extreme cold and equipment failure for the delays that led to concerns voiced by the Japan Food Agency.
Both railways were considering using one rail line through British Columbia's avalanche-prone Fraser Valley to ship grain in one direction, Vanclief said.
The other firm's rail line would be used to expedite the return of hopper cars back to the interior, he added.
The CWB alleged grain movement was a low priority for the railways.
